newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Thwarted Albania opposition calls city shutdown.
newsitem.headline: Thwarted Albania opposition calls city shutdown.

text.p: Opponents of Albania's right-wing government, their attempts to demonstrate in Tirana thwarted by police, urged disgruntled residents on Sunday to switch to passive protests and shut down the city each day at lunchtime.

The opposition's spiritual leader, imprisoned since 1994 on corruption charges, blamed President Sali Berisha for the collapse of pyramid investment schemes and called on Albanians to join forces against the ruling Democratic Party.

Tens of thousands staged a fifth day of protests in the southern port of Vlore. But the failure to stage a rally in the capital prompted a change of tactics by the opposition Forum for Democracy alliance.
"The Forum calls on the people to demonstrate peacefully every day from 12 p.m. to 2 p.m in any form," it said in a statement printed in Tirana newspapers.
"Gather silently on pavements, demonstrate with a slice of bread in your hand, close down shops, boycott classrooms, sound your car horns."
A day after riot police chased demonstrators away from Tirana's Skanderbeg Square, the area was bustling with shoppers examining wares at dishevelled pavement stalls.
A dozen police vans maintained a conspicuous presence and riot police in khaki uniforms lounged nearby.
State television showed Berisha strolling through the square and congratulating the nation's large Moslem community for the end of the month of Ramadan.
In Vlore, 30,000 protesters again marched down the city's main boulevard to press for the return of lost savings and the government's resignation.

The Forum's 10 parties hold Berisha responsible for the collapse of pyramid funds in which virtually every family has tied up savings in post-Communist Albania. It wants talks with the president to form a "technocrat government".

Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu, who heads the Democrats, offered to meet opposition parties later this week to discuss the pyramid crisis. The Forum rejected a similar offer last week and it was not clear if it would accept the new proposal.
Jailed Socialist leader Fatos Nano, in an appeal printed in the daily Koha Jone, gave his blessing to the newly-created Forum as the vehicle for confronting the president.

"The plundering of Albanians is a result of Berisha's capitalism without banks, systematic violation of human rights and the transformation of democratic institutions into presidential preserves," he said.
"I urge Berisha to call military units back to barracks, stop the terror and arrests and accept dialogue with the real opposition to the benefit of Albania's interests."

Nano was twice prime minister of Albania, but his second term after the 1991 fall of communism was ended by a general strike. He was jailed in 1994 on corruption charges but the former supreme court chairman who sentenced him now says he was innocent and the opposition sees him as a political prisoner.

The opposition said police had detained 15 of its leaders briefly during Saturday's abortive Tirana rally and one activist with a large welt on his forehead said he had been severely beaten. Several reporters were also attacked.
The government denied that oppostion activists had been rounded up or beaten and Berisha issued a statement denouncing all violence associated with protests.
Enraged investors set fire to buildings in several towns last month. Mass arrests kept protesters off streets for a time and authorities began partial refunds for investors in two failed schemes.
